recent_posts.title: Claude Opus 4.7 is not the milestone Anthropic wants you to think it is
recent_posts.summary: A skeptical take on Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.7 release, arguing it's not a significant milestone. Key points covered: benchmark improvements are modest and AI benchmarks can be gamed; the 'adaptive thinking' feature (where Claude decides whether to use extended thinking rather than the user) is criticized as potentially a cost-saving measure; the updated tokenizer uses ~35% more tokens raising cost concerns despite unchanged prices; new cybersecurity safeguards are causing false positives for legitimate developers; Anthropic's recent PR struggles around rate limits and transparency; and comparisons to OpenAI's Codex as competitive pressure. The author's overall view is that Opus 4.5 was arguably better in practice, and this release is incremental at best.

recent_posts.title: Competition Is A Good Thing
recent_posts.summary: Competition between companies is real and should be embraced rather than downplayed. Despite public narratives that frame rivals as friendly co-participants, companies are genuinely competing for alternate visions of the world. Like sports teams, competitors can respect each other while still wanting to win decisively. Denying the competitive nature of business is dishonest — there are real winners and losers, and acknowledging that drive is healthy.

recent_posts.title: AI has permanently changed how we program
recent_posts.summary: A personal take on how AI has fundamentally changed programming, arguing that November marked an inflection point where AI tools became transformative regardless of future improvements. The author believes programming still requires significant human input and understanding, but the landscape has shifted permanently. Using tools like Claude Code delivers most of their value quickly, though deeper value requires more expertise.

recent_posts.title: Why every developer needs a mental checklist when writing code
recent_posts.summary: Competent developers maintain a mental checklist when writing code, regardless of whether it's AI-generated or handwritten. Key questions include: Are we solving the correct problem? Are we solving it correctly? Are there edge cases or gaps in understanding? The concern is that over-reliance on AI and copy-pasting is eroding these fundamental habits, especially among newer developers who skipped learning the basics.

recent_posts.title: Skepticism around claims that developers no longer write code from scratch
recent_posts.summary: A developer pushes back on claims that writing code from scratch is dead. They argue that agentic AI coding tools aren't great for code review, and that manually typing code is itself part of the design thinking process — helping developers figure out function relationships and folder structure. They draw a parallel to past tech hype cycles where people claimed a new tool changed everything, but the resulting products often didn't exist or weren't better than before. The skepticism extends to products built entirely with AI, which often feel lower quality.

recent_posts.title: Claude Code source code accidentally leaked via source maps
recent_posts.summary: Anthropic accidentally exposed Claude Code's source maps during a routine update, making the TypeScript/Bun-based codebase temporarily readable. Key findings from the leaked code include: anti-distillation systems targeting competitors, silent profanity logging, unreleased features, and evidence of borrowed scroll behavior from the open-source OpenCode project. A Python port of the leaked code was created using OpenAI's Codex, raising unresolved legal questions about whether AI-generated code can be copyrighted and whether Anthropic can DMCA the port. The incident also highlights the tension between the Claude Code team's 'move fast with AI agents' philosophy and traditional code review practices.

recent_posts.title: How LLM dependence erodes developer coding skills over time
recent_posts.summary: A developer reflects on how relying on LLMs for coding tasks is gradually eroding their technical skills, drawing a parallel to losing mental math ability after becoming dependent on calculators. They note that while LLMs handle routine coding, there are moments when manual intervention is needed and it 'doesn't feel good' — feeling less capable than before. The broader question raised is whether the cognitive energy saved by AI tools is being redirected productively or simply wasted on passive consumption like scrolling TikTok while Codex runs.

recent_posts.title: Clean Code is More Important than Ever
recent_posts.summary: LLMs can't distinguish between old and new coding patterns in a codebase, so they tend to replicate outdated approaches. This makes maintaining a clean, consistent codebase more critical than ever — because AI tools will blindly follow whatever patterns they find, good or bad. Teams are now more motivated to establish clear, intentional patterns and ensure every file adheres to them.

recent_posts.title: Why combining coding with domain expertise unlocks career breakthroughs
recent_posts.summary: Coding skills alone have a ceiling on career growth. Developers who break through to the top 1% typically combine strong programming ability with deep expertise in a second domain, such as finance or another industry. This dual expertise creates a unique vantage point to spot overlooked gaps and opportunities that others miss, enabling outsized career impact.

recent_posts.title: Most technical debt comes from inexperience not intentional trade-offs
recent_posts.summary: Most technical debt isn't the result of intentional trade-offs made under time pressure — it's largely a skill issue. When developers claim they made deliberate trade-offs to move fast, the reality is that roughly 95% of the resulting mess stems from inexperience or being overwhelmed, not conscious decisions. The next time the same problem is tackled with more experience, most of those 'trade-offs' disappear naturally.
